extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and constructing inductive inferences, the law of causation, identification of natural kinds, and related logical/probabilistic reasoning used in the sciences. Emphasizes what experience can legitimately establish and common pitfalls in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of induction / limited uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction (e.g. 'fire burns') does not require that all nature observe uniform laws, but only that there should be uniformity in one particular class of natural phenomena; generalizations do not imply uniformity pervading all nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The uniformity required for an inductive conclusion is only that which exists within the observed class and as much of that same uniformity beyond it as corresponds to the observed instances. Example: 'fire burns' needs only uniformity among phenomena related to fire, not universal natural uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation is empirical, not a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causation is not known a priori; it is itself a conclusion from experience rather than a presupposed universal principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat causation as an independent, self-evident truth beyond the reach of empirical verification. Critiques that assert causal laws are 'transcendental' are challenged: causation's universality must be supported by accumulated experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction does not prove universality beyond experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract conceptions elicited from experience cannot be evidence of an objective fact in universal Nature beyond what the experience itself bears witness to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skeptical of claims that a faculty of abstraction can justify universal truths not contained in experience; abstraction may analyze observed elements but cannot validly extend evidence beyond experiential limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific conclusions are conditional on uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: When physical science is said to depend on the assumption that the course of nature is invariable, it means scientific conclusions are conditional—not absolute—truths: their truth is conditional on the uniformity of the course of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical conduct, conditional conclusiveness (truth provided current laws remain valid) suffices. Recognize and state the conditional nature of scientific claims rather than claiming absolute certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling / 'promiscuous' situation of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive inferences are justified (with high probability) when observed cases are 'situated promiscuously' — i.e., when the observed instances are representative and not systematically biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies like the desert chambers: even a comparatively small number of randomly distributed observed cases can justify acting on a presumption until an exception appears. Emphasize representativeness rather than raw quantity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of nature grounded in observed agencies and sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The uniformity of the course of nature as a whole is constituted by the uniform sequences of special effects from special natural agencies; many such agencies have been made sufficiently amenable to observation to ascertain fixed laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue for global uniformity by aggregating evidence about distinct causes and their regular sequences rather than appealing to an abstract universal principle. This addresses objections that the number of natural agents is 'incalculably large.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles interpreted as new antecedent causes, not law violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged miracles are not exceptions to the law of causation; in each case a new antecedent (a counteracting cause, e.g., supernatural volition) is affirmed to exist, so the event is a case of causation rather than a deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating testimony of extraordinary events, consider whether the explanation posits an additional antecedent cause rather than assuming a breach of causation; this reframes miracles within causal reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifying inferences about the future by analogy with past/future-as-past
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of future facts is analogous to knowledge of unobserved past facts: though we had no experience of what is future, we have had abundant experience of what was future (i.e., became present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that presumption about future resemblance to past is psychological, but that subsequent verification by experience yields the logical proof. Use verification of past-future analogues as the standard for justifying expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of uniformity and law of causation (universality implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no other uniformity in events of nature than that which arises from the law of causation; if the uniformity of the course of nature has any exceptions, to that extent the law of causation fails (i.e., some events would have no causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit: doubting global uniformity entails doubting the universality (not the reality) of causation. Use this to frame discussions about possible exceptions and the logical consequences for causal theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of Natural Kinds requires conjunction of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually several properties are required to identify a Kind; each property singly may be shared with other Kinds, but together they mark the Kind (e.g., diamond identified by color, brightness, octahedral form together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reliance on single hallmark features when classifying natural kinds; require conjunctions of properties and remain open to further unascertained properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of Induction apply to chemical composition and special sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases of chemical composition are cases of causation and therefore fall under the general Canons of Induction; special adaptations for particular sciences belong to the logic of the special sciences, not to General Logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing methods for specific sciences (e.g., chemistry), adapt general inductive canons appropriately, but do not treat them as exceptions to the general principles of causation and induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of inference from approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: From two approximate generalizations (e.g., 'Most A are B' and 'Most A are C') we may infer with certainty only limited conclusions (e.g., that some B are C); approximate premises set strict limits on what can be drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-extend conclusions from imprecise or approximate premises; be explicit about the maximal logically defensible inference (e.g., De Morgan's remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability theory grounded in causes' frequency and efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of frequency of a coincidence measures the frequency combined with the efficacy of the causes favoring it; when multiple causes operate, analyze their combined efficacy to evaluate probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer causal analysis over naive combinatorial counting when assessing chances. The illustrative calculation (As and Cs producing Bs) shows how combined causal operation raises the expected frequency (e.g., arriving at 11/12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer essential, characteristic definitions to avoid extra axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should capture the attribute really involved (e.g., define parallel lines by equidistance rather than 'in the same plane and never meeting') to avoid the need for additional axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining terms, choose properties that express the essential meaning to minimize auxiliary assumptions and the burden of extra axioms in subsequent reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility defined relative to complete induction
rubrics_metrics.description: An impossibility is that the truth of which would conflict with a complete induction — that is, with the most conclusive evidence which we possess of universal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat many 'reputed impossibilities' as provisional (e.g., high-speed travel, painless surgery once thought impossible). Reserve the label 'impossible' for propositions incompatible with a complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate testimony by combining event frequencies and witness error
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing credibility (e.g., reports of particular draws), consider both the frequency of the events and the witness's veracity/error rates; naive ratios can be misleading without this analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete probabilistic accounting (as in the ball-drawing example) to compute credibility ratios rather than relying on simplistic multiplicative intuitions (corrects the 999:1 misapprehension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate or false conceptions when explaining phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying inappropriate conceptions (or wholly false conceptions with no prototype in nature) leads to failure in explanation (e.g., misapplying properties of circles to lever mechanics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the conceptual tools/methods used to explain a phenomenon have real counterparts in the facts; check for both inappropriateness (wrong frame) and falsity (no real prototype).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language not a necessary condition for belief or inductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions necessary to enable reasoning (induction) are senses and association; language is not asserted to be a necessary precondition for belief or reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between powers (reasoning, belief) and their conditions; avoid the mistaken interpretation that denying language's necessity implies a reductionist analysis of the faculties themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: General names evoke representative ideas useful for class reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a class calls up some idea (sometimes of one individual, sometimes composite) by which we can carry on inductions and ratiocination about the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class-names as cognitive tools that evoke representative mental images which support inductive reasoning, while recognizing they're not perfect substitutes for the underlying observational basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and avoid common inferential fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of fallacies such as à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter (fallacia accidentis) and converse fallacies (à dicto simpliciter ad dictum secundum quid); these errors misapply general/special statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical examples and formal awareness (De Morgan, etc.) to detect when a general rule is inappropriately specialized or a qualified statement is illegitimately generalized. Example caution: do not infer 'strong drink is a cause of strength' from superficial association.
